en: Zulpukor, inherited from his father Manas,
Was fastened upon his forearm.
The coat of mail made by Kanykei
Was fitted firmly upon his chest.
Akkelte, inherited from Manas,
Hung across his broad back.
Akolpok, inherited from Manas,
Was worn by Kulchoro.
When he drew near the maidens,
Kulchoro was like a vast sea;
At the sight of him, minds were overwhelmed.
He appeared like a prince,
Glancing to either side;
Your gray-maned one, like a hungry tiger,
Licked his lips.
He wore a golden belt;
Of that surpassingly handsome young man,
Sunlight struck his moonlike face.
At the sight of him, minds were overwhelmed.
His figure and his majesty,
His bearing mounted on the horse,
Appeared like Ala-Too.
The maidens who saw him
Lost all command of their senses.
When they saw the young man's form,
He seemed capable of carrying them all away,
Of taking them together to his home.
He came ambling in a stately line
Aichurok's white pavilion—
He went and took shelter there.
There they whispered together,
Teasing one another and laughing;
Some fled at a run,
Despairing of their precious lives.
They stood as though harboring guilty thoughts,
Their mouths muttering;
They looked at one another,
Moved their lips without being heard,
And whispered among themselves:
"Will he fondle us after manhandling us?
Will he take us all together to his home?
Will the offspring of that coarse khan
Seize us as plunder and carry us
Together to Talas?
May God strike the brute!
Will he make us captive wives?"
Thinking this, the maidens and brides
Cried loudly enough for God to hear;
They pressed close against one another,
And, as though slaughter had struck them,
Collapsed and fell together.
Kulchoro was twelve years old.
Upon the red horse Buurul,
The rascal came moving sleekly,
Calm and ringing with vigor.
Thirty brides and thirty maidens,
All those souls swarming there,
He did not value as much as his boot-tip.
Though still a boy, the courage
That Almighty Allah had given him
Was beyond all measure.
Upon the red horse Buurul,
He rode at an angle,
Throwing the maidens and brides into panic.
To test and learn his courage,
Beside a steep ravine with a flowing spring,
A wretched woman, burning with passion, said:
"If he has courage, he will ride on
And trample straight across," she said,
"If he is fainthearted, he will skirt the edge
And slip past from the side," she said.
To satisfy the hearts of all who watched,
That unfortunate sister-in-law of yours
Had rugs and quilts together
Spread for the length of a spear as a barrier.
All the maidens and brides
She startled and made sport of;
The quilts and rugs she had laid down
She made him ride over and trample,
As though they were spread upon the open road.
That same Churok thought:
"His forefathers before his father—
Will the offspring of that insolent line
Ride heedlessly across?
Will he shout, 'Come here, falcon!'
And, babbling wildly, carry all
The people of Akun to their ruin?"
Her moonlike face appeared;
The hem of her many-colored gown
Showed in wondrous beauty.
From among those maidens,
Gleaming as though moonlight struck her,
Your Churok, the daughter of Akun,
Stepped out alone.
As she walked, her face shone;
A little golden amulet
Rang upon her breast.
When she glanced around suddenly,
The human heart was overwhelmed.
Standing poised and serene,
She appeared like a peri.
She walked smiling and radiant;
Sixty clasps and forty pearl buttons
Glittered at her throat.
Fragrance wafted, and brass ornaments turned;
She smiled, overwhelming the heart.
A blue-lynx and beaver hat
Was visible upon the brow
Of that poor daughter of Akun.
Your extraordinarily beautiful sister-in-law
Had words sweeter than sugar.
Whoever saw her lost all sense;
Above her lip
She had a small beauty mark.
In what part could this doomed Churok
Possibly be found lacking?
If a man happened to see her,
The poor swaggering wretch,
If he were to behold your sister-in-law,
Might die before he reached Issyk-Kul.
To the young man riding the red horse Buurul,
Coming at an angle,
Your sister-in-law stretched forward and cried,
Calling, "Wait there!"
Veering like a swift horse,
Your grieving sister-in-law began to speak:
"Hey, boy! Turn your horse's head;
Stand there in the open place ahead!"
She waved and beckoned with her hand;
Aichurok, proud as a rooster,
Flung a taunt at him:
"My boy, turn your horse's head;
Stand there in the open place ahead!
Who is your battle cry, and what is your name?
You have dressed yourself splendidly;
Who are the in-laws joined to you by marriage?
My boy, do not break custom without cause.
If you are a traveler, here is the road;
If you are a raider, here is the livestock!
If you are thirsty, here is water;
If you wander seeking beauty, my dear,
Here are we, the beauties who pine!
If you would lie down, here is a tent and bed;
If you would make merry, here are we!
My boy, your Argyn and Kyrgyz people
Are nowhere here;
As though mounted upon your finest horse,
As though wearing your own coat,
Do not swagger without cause!
You ride over the rugs laid down;
This deed of yours is no small thing.
As though you and your elder brother
Might trample and ride away over them—
These are not Kyrgyz maidens.
Boy, what is it you have sent flying?
Tell me your circumstances fully:
Who is it you mean to fight?
What is it you have lost?
Who is it you wage war against?
What village have you approached in courtship?
Who are the in-laws joined to you by marriage?"
As Churok stood speaking thus,
The sea-like Choro began to answer:
"If taunting words are fine,
I shall test their strength;
Taunting you with proper skill,
I shall strike every bone in your body.
If you act beyond all propriety,
I shall bring you all to ruin;
I shall raid the village
Of your father, gray-maned Akun.
If the Afghans prove unruly,
I shall plunder their finest goods
And deal harshly with the rebels.
Thirty brides and thirty maidens,
You lie here making sport;
I understand the purpose of what you have done:
You have come to welcome splendidly
Your bridegroom named Semetey!
I understand your purpose well:
You have come out into the street to welcome
Your bridegroom, lion-like Semetey!
I know your measure.
When the time comes for me to die,
I am a slave worth no more than a dog's hide.
If you ask my true origin,
I am the son of the Chinese Almambet;
I tell you the truth as I stand here:
I am Semetey's servant!
Do not trouble me, sister-in-law;

en: Agree to what I say.
You should not mock
A man whose head is bound by duty;
Give me Akshumkar!
Let me strip the weariness from my horse,
And fly throughout
The whole wide world.
At the edge of Ala-Kol,
You changed into a white swan;
So that you might somehow find a husband,
Semetey's Akshumkar
You carried away!
What I sent flying was Akshumkar;
The man I will fight is brave Toltoi.
What I lost was Akshumkar;
The man I war against is Chynkojo.
If it is a matter of kinship, Khan Akun is our in-law;
I shall speak closely with Ajybai,
And cross weapons with Tumenbai.
Yesterday, at Kokotoy's memorial feast,
With gray-maned Manas at the head,
When multitudes gathered and the people clamored,
When infidel and Muslim
Swarmed like worms,
And the spectacle reached its height,
Khan Akun, khan of the Afghans,
Was a khan possessed of sacred power;
He had given his promise
To Manas as a sworn in-law.
You speak too many words, sister-in-law,
And make me babble far too much.
What inheritance will you gain
By making mockery of a servant?
Why should I listen to your taunts?
Give me the falcon, and let me go!
The mount beneath me
Is Semetey's courser;
What I lost and wander seeking
Is my bloodthirsty lord's falcon!
Do not turn my errand into ridicule;
Do not idly mock
A man whose head is bound by duty!
What I wear upon me
Is my poor lord's Akolpok;
Though worn by a servant,
The armor fits Kulchoro exactly.
The coat I wear belongs to another,
The horse I ride belongs to another;
My uncle, who might strike in a fury,
Is in a dangerous temper.
Now agree to what I have said;
Do not mock me, dear sister-in-law,
And give me the falcon now.
What wish can I fulfill
By trading words with maidens?
Dear sister-in-law, give it now,
And let me take the falcon away!"
When Choro had spoken thus,
Churok stood and said:
"Oh, what shameless nonsense!
Your Argyn and Kyrgyz people are not here.
You are young, my dear;
Do not carry on without cause!
You have accused me of ranging
